text:
And now Effi detached the wafer seal and read: “Most highly honored madam,
most gracious Baroness! Permit me to add a most humble request to my most respectful morning greetings. A dear friend of mine of many years’ standing, a daughter of our Good Town of Kessin, Miss Marietta Trippelli, will arrive here on the midday train and remain among us until tomorrow morning. She intends to be in Petersburg on the seventeenth, to give concerts there until the middle of January. Prince Kotschukoff is once again opening his hospitable house to her. In her unfailing kindness toward me, Trippelli has promised to spend this evening at my home and to perform several songs entirely of my choosing (for she knows no difficulties). Might the Baroness be prevailed upon to attend this musical evening? Seven o’clock. Your husband, on whose appearance I confidently rely, will support my most humble request. Present will be only Pastor Lindequist (who will accompany her) and, of course, the widowed Pastor’s wife Trippel. With the most distinguished devotion, A. Gieshübler.”

“Well—,” said Innstetten, “yes or no?”

“Of course yes. That will take me out of myself. And besides, I cannot turn down my dear Gieshübler at his very first invitation.”

“Agreed. So, Friedrich, tell Mirambo, who presumably brought the note, that we would have the honor.” Friedrich left.

When he had gone, Effi asked: “Who is Mirambo?”

“The real Mirambo is a robber chieftain in Africa—Lake Tanganyika, if your geography extends that far—but ours is merely Gieshübler’s coal-yard manager and factotum, and will very probably wait upon us this evening in tails and cotton gloves.”

It was quite evident that the little incident had had a favorable effect on Effi and restored a good deal of her lightheartedness, but Innstetten wished to do his part to advance this convalescence. “I am glad that you said yes, and so quickly and without hesitation, and now I should like to make you another suggestion, to set you entirely to rights again. I can see that something from last night is still haunting you, something that does not suit my Effi, something that simply must go away again, and there is nothing better for that than fresh air. The weather is magnificent, fresh and mild at the same time, with scarcely a breath of wind; what do you say to our taking a drive, but a long one, not merely through the plantation, and in the sleigh, of course, with the bells on and the white snow blankets, and then, when we are back at four, you can rest, and at seven we shall be at Gieshübler’s and hear Trippelli.”

Effi took his hand. “How good you are, Geert, and how forbearing. For I must have seemed childish to you, or at least very childlike; first with my fear, and then afterward, asking you to sell the house and, what is worse still, that business with the Prince. You are to put his chair outside the door—it is laughable. For after all, he is the man who decides our fate. Mine too. You cannot imagine how ambitious I am. I really married you solely out of ambition. But you must not look so serious at that. I do love you . . . what is it called again, when one breaks off a twig and plucks off the leaves? With all my heart, with all its smart, beyond all measure.”

And she laughed brightly. “And now tell me,” she continued, when Innstetten still remained silent, “where are we to go?” “I had thought to the railway station, but by a roundabout route, and then back along the highway. And we shall eat at the station, or better still at Golchowski’s, at the ‘Prince Bismarck’ inn, which we passed on the day of our arrival, if you perhaps remember. Making such an appearance always has a good effect, and then I shall have an election talk with the starosta by Effi’s grace, and though he is not worth much personally, he keeps his establishment in order and his kitchen in even better order. The people here know about eating and drinking.”

It was close to eleven when they had this conversation. At twelve Kruse drew up before the door with the sleigh, and Effi got in. Johanna wanted to bring the foot muff and furs, but after everything that still weighed upon her, Effi felt such a need for fresh air that she refused them all and took only a double blanket. Innstetten, however, said to Kruse: “Kruse, we are now going to the railway station, where the two of us have already been once this morning. People will be surprised, but that does no harm. I think we shall drive along the plantation here and then turn left toward the Kroschentin church tower. Let the horses run. We must be at the station by one.”

And so the drive began. Smoke hung above the town’s white roofs, for there was little movement in the air. Utpatel’s mill too was turning only slowly, and they sped past it, close beside the churchyard, whose barberry bushes grew out over the railings and brushed Effi with their tips, so that snow fell onto her carriage rug. On the other side of the road was an enclosed plot, not much larger than a garden bed, and within it nothing was visible but a young pine rising from its center.

“Is someone buried there too?” Effi asked. “Yes, the Chinaman.”

Effi started; it felt like a stab. But she still had enough strength to control herself and asked with apparent calm:

“Ours?”

“Yes, ours. Naturally, he could not be accommodated in the municipal churchyard, and so Captain Thomsen, who was something like a friend of his, bought this plot and had him buried here. There is also a stone with an inscription. All before my time, of course. But people still talk about it.”

“So there is something to it after all. A story. You said something like that earlier this morning. And in the end it will be best if I hear what it is. As long as I do not know, despite all my good intentions, I am still a victim of my imaginings. Tell me what really happened. Reality cannot torment me as much as my imagination.”

“Bravo, Effi. I did not want to speak of it. But now it has come about of its own accord, and that is good. Besides, it is really nothing at all.”
